title: TA8-08535
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: These are the reasons I reject the refugee claims of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, (herein known as the claimant) a 53 year old citizen of Colombia.

In addition, I reject the joined claims of his 24 year old son, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his 52 year old wife, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and his three daughters, 27 year old XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, 23 year old XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and 21 year old XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, all citizens of Colombia. Allegations:
The claimant alleges that while he worked for a XXXX XXXX XXXX and also as an XXXX XXXX, he had problems with the paramilitary group AUC and its successor the Black Eagles.

After refusing to pay the extortion demands the claimant fled Colombia in XXXX 2008. The rest of his family left Colombia in XXXX 2008. After short stays in the United States (US), the family came to Canada and made refugee claims. Determination
I found the claimant to be not a credible witness. Since all the claims rely on the case of the claimant, all the claims fail. Analysis

When questioned as to when his problems with the paramilitaries began the claimant responded in XXXX 2006 he had to leave the area. Orally, he spoke of the group asking him to provide vehicles and road building machinery. He was asked what else was requested. He responded that if he did not follow their instructions he would be killed but nothing else was demanded in XXXX 2006. When it was pointed out later that in the report filed in XXXX 2006, Exhibit C-13, item 1, when speaking of the XXXX 2006 problems, it tells of being asked to XXXX equipment but makes no mention of demands to lend equipment such as XXXX XXXX XXXX, the claimant responded that not all the information was put in the report since you do not know who you are speaking with. The claimant was asked why the report states they demanded money in XXXX 2006 and this was not mentioned in his oral evidence. The claimant did not provide an explanation but instead spoke of being an employee and not handling money for the company.

If the claimant's problems began in XXXX 2006 when the groups demanded he lend the equipment as he stated orally, then I would expect this to be consistent in both his Personal Information Form (Exhibit C-1) narrative and in the police report. (Exhibit C-13, item 1).

In the original PIF narrative there is no mention of a report to the Attorney General. When asked to explain the claimant stated he was concentrating on the events of XXXX 2008. The instructions for the preparations of the narrative are clear that all efforts to seek protection are to be included. Since the claimant signed the first copy of his PIF that he understood it and it was complete, if there was a report made in XXXX 2006 it should have been included a that time. It should not have been necessary to make an amendment 10 months later.

The report speaks of repairing equipment and demands for money, since neither of these were indicated in oral evidence I am satisfied that the account of problems with the groups and the account of making a report was created to advance his refugee claim.

The claimant initially testified that his next problems occurred in 2008. When questioned directly, regarding 2007, he remembered that a message was left with a worker on a project at the beginning of 2007, that they wanted to speak to me. The claimant explained that to contact them they would come back. He was not to do anything and this is normal, they just indicate they want to talk to someone. He was asked why the Black Eagles would send a message without instructions i.e. a phone number or a place to meet and yet never come to talk to him. The claimant's only explanation for such a strange message was so the person will find a way to get in touch. He explained he believed he was expected to ask in the area where the Black Eagles were located and how to contact them.

I find, on a balance of probabilities, it is implausible that the claimant would be given a message that the Black Eagles wanted to talk to him and yet provide no way to contact them nor was there any attempt from the Black Eagles to contact the claimant. His explanation that he would be expected to find the Black Eagles by asking in the community where they lived is not reasonable. It assumes people know who the Black Eagles are and the claimant would approach them. I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, this account of a message from the Black Eagles is again, not credible.

The XXXX, 2008 report, Exhibit C-13, item 3, states the claimant was attacked by armed men in XXXX 2006. When asked if this happened the claimant initially evaded the question by responding if it says that, it must have happened. The claimant then stated this was in 2008. When asked to explain why if there was a XXXX 2006 incident, it was not included in the PIF narrative. The claimant suggested that perhaps the word in the report should have been "approached" not attacked.
In addition, the date of the 2008 attack is reported as XXXX, 2008 in the report. In his amended PIF he indicates it should have been XXXX and the error was due to nervousness.

I don't accept these explanations. The original report filed with the Attorney General just prior to leaving Colombia, according to the claimant's latter evidence was written by the claimant, in Spanish, on April 2 and delivered to the Attorney General on April 4. That being the case it should have accurately described his problems with the illegal groups.

Since the information in the report is inconsistent with his oral and written evidence, on a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied the claimant created the information in the report to the Attorney General filed prior to leaving Colombia. Again, the actions show a willingness to create evidence in Colombia and swear to its truthfulness to advance his refugee claim in Canada.

When questioned as to the purpose of the April report, the claimant testified he wanted to leave a record that something was happening to me. He claimed that he wanted protection but knew he was not going to get protection. The claimant explained the report is dated April 2, 2008 and was not taken to the Attorney General Office until April 4. The evidence, as pointed out in the hearing room, is that the report was received by the Attorney General at 3:40 pm on April 4. The claimant's passport shows he cleared security at the airport at 10 pm that same day.

The final sentence of the report is a clear request for help. The claimant asks the assigned prosecutor to advise him what he should do since his life and the lives of his family members are at risk. If the claimant was truly asking for help and was fearful for his life, I am satisfied he would not have waited a month after the attack, and then make a report just 6 hours before clearing exit control at the airport to catch a 12:00 flight to Toronto, Canada. On a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied the claimant was not fearful for his life when he left Colombia.

The claimant, in his third amended PIF, exhibit C-14, outlines that a man asked for information about his wife's relatives from a woman who sold phone cards near his mother- in-law's home. In his oral evidence, the claimant stated that the vendor was asked if she had seen people who looked like members of the claimant's family. Both counsel and myself, asked for details as to how this could occur since there was no indication the woman was shown pictures of the claimant. The claimant spoke of the Black Eagles having people all over and the vendors of phone cards see people. The claimant never answered how the vendor was to know what the family looked like or even that the armed person asked by name. Further, at the end of the hearing, the claimant's counsel asked the wife for any information omitted by her husband. The claimant's wife indicated that the vendor told her sister about being approached and asked for information about the family. When I asked the claimant how he knew armed men had questioned the vendor in the phone card booth, he had not indicated the vendor had told his sister-in-law, the claimant attempted to correct me by stating he had not said the men were armed. His earlier evidence was that the men were armed.

All this information as to how the family knew of the vendor being approached should have been provided in oral evidence when the claimant was asked for details. If it was the claimant's wife who was told about the vendor being approached, this information should have been provided in her amended PIF.

It is not plausible that armed men would suddenly start questioning a vendor about the family in the area of the claimant's mother-in-law unless they already knew that was where his relatives lived. If they had that information, they would know the mother-in-law's address and there would be no reason to question the vendor.

The story of stopping the nephew is equally problematic. Counsel questioned how they, the Black Eagles, could find the nephew? The response was they asked a woman who sells phone cards about the family. It was never explained to me how this would allow the representatives of the Black Eagles to connectt any one to the family. The only way this account could possibly make any sense would be if they showed the vendor photos of claimant and there is no evidence this occurred. Hence I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities; this account again has been created for this hearing to advance the claimant's refugee claim. Summary:

The XXXX 2006 report is inconsistent with the claimant's other evidence. The claimant's evidence that the Black Eagles wanted to speak to him was initially omitted from his oral evidence and is implausible since no contact method was provided.
The April 2008 report is not consistent with the oral and written statements of the claimant.
The account of the vendor being approached for family information is inconsistent as to whether the person was armed and is implausible on its face. Conclusion:

For all of the above, I find the claimant was not a credible witness. Since many of his credibility concerns occur due to his supporting documents, I give these documents insufficient weight to advance the claim on their own.

All the related claims rely on the evidence of the claimant. I am satisfied the claimants failed to establish there is a serious possibility they will be persecuted or suffer other forms of serious harm should they return to Colombia today.

The Refugee Protection Division rejects the claims pursuant to both sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
